records.name: Bourgogne-Franche-Comté
records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Dijon / Cote-d'Or: rural traditional department. Regional evidence: the only prefecture in the country found to have twice banned a Pride march from its city centre with the ban upheld - on 12 June 2025 the prefecture prohibited the Pride 2025 march in central Dijon citing "risk of trouble to public order", the second consecutive year of the same restriction; the organisers' withdrawal citing LGBT visibility was itself called significant by the city. On 14 June 2025 the administrative court rejected the legal challenge, and the march (about 1,500 people per police) proceeded on a diverted route around the historic centre; the prefecture justified the ban by estimated organiser numbers (200 vs previous 2,500 and 1,500 turnouts) and a stated risk of violent individuals attaching themselves. The march itself passed peacefully ("joyful and festive, without a hitch") - the harm documented here is the restriction and its chilling effect, not violence. Scored relative to the national score (0.67) for France.

records.name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
records.summary: Region research direction: mixed — the country's largest LGBTQ+ community and its biggest police raids coexist, with police acting without legal basis. (1) 1 February 2025: police arrested 56 men at a hotel in the capital at a reported "gay sex party"; organisers risk pornography-law prosecution with penalties up to 15 years; Amnesty International Indonesia called the police's "discriminatory and senseless harassment of LGBTI people ... has no basis in law" and demanded release of those detained. (2) One of the eight provinces where an international NGO found discriminatory regional regulations — and simultaneously the city with the country's densest LGBTQ+ infrastructure, media presence and monitoring-group offices; an assessor should expect both to be true at once. National climate from this record's sources: an October 2025 presidential decree listed "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among the country's non-military national security threats alongside terrorism and drugs, amplifying self-censorship (editors killing LGBTQ+ stories for fear of state reprisal); police deny violence and extortions in the 2022 death-in-custody of a US-based trans activist arrested on drug charges at Bali airport while family members allege he was beaten. Model-estimate residual (route 3, best-knowledge delta): sheer scale of the community limits enforcement reach.

records.name: Quintana Roo
records.summary: Quintana Roo: worse than national for what a visitor actually meets — the country's main tourist corridor, with a documented policing problem. The Cancún/Riviera Maya hotel zone is a massive international tourism envelope with a commercially gay-friendly surface, but municipal and state police have been repeatedly documented committing discriminatory acts against LGBT+ people, with multiple recorded assaults during detention concentrated in Tulum and Playa del Carmen; the community describes officers as untrained in human-rights standards. The municipal Directorate for Sexual Diversity recorded three formal discrimination complaints in a single year, including violence against a transgender woman, and two Tourist Police members were fired after their own body cameras showed them running an extortion ring against visitors with portable card terminals. Cancún's immigration detention facility is documented as a place of systematic rights violations with no accountability — relevant to a visitor whose documents are questioned. Countervailing: the state enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and banned conversion practices in December 2023. Scored relative to the national score (0.55) for Mexico.
